The Gemara in Menachos records a dispute over whether tzitzis is an obligation resting on the individual or an obligation resting on the garment itself. On the first view a person is bound only when he actually wears a four-cornered garment; on the second view every four-cornered garment in his possession must be fitted with tzitzis even while it sits unused. Tosfos narrows the practical stake to that stored garment and stresses that both sides agree nobody must go out and buy a four-cornered garment. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch rule that the obligation rests on the person, so a man who owns tzitzis is still not compelled to put them on. At the same time they warn that wearing a four-cornered garment without tzitzis means neglecting a positive commandment, and they urge diligence in a mitzvah that keeps the commandments constantly in mind.

Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach makes weaving the test: synthetic fibre spun into thread and woven into a four-cornered garment carries the obligation and takes a bracha, while a single moulded sheet is exempt like leather. Rav Moshe disagrees, holding that synthetics stay leather-like even when woven, because the material can be produced without weaving at all; he therefore rules against buying such tzitzis and against reciting a bracha on them. His grandson records a qualification: if polyester is in fact always spun into thread first, the leather comparison collapses and a rabbinic obligation returns. The Or L’Tzion and the Halacha Berura, joined by Rav Elyashiv, advise avoiding synthetic tzitzis and withholding the bracha. The subject is approached as a weighing exercise rather than a search for one knockout proof. Because no argument on either side is conclusive, the outcome rests on the cumulative force of many sugyos and Rishonim leaning in one direction. This mirrors the Ramban, who opened his critique of the Baal Hamaor by admitting that individual questions could be answered, and who committed instead to careful analysis of both sides before judging which position was more convincing. Rav Moshe supplies the second half of the method: talmidei chachomim who understand shas and poskim are obligated to apply their own reasoning to new questions, even where the result conflicts with some acharonim, provided they are not overturning Rishonim who are quoted for halacha by the Shulchan Aruch and the Rama. Indigo and the murex dye differ only in that two hydrogen atoms of indigo are replaced by two bromine atoms, producing dibromoindigo and a purple rather than blue color. When the murex dye is reduced with an alkaline base it becomes soluble and yellow, and sunlight at that stage strips away the bromine, leaving a molecule chemically identical to indigo. This matches the Gemara that says only Hashem can tell techeiles apart from the plant dye called kala ilan, which the Aruch and Nimukei Yosef render as indigo, since the two blues are literally the same molecule. The Shulchan Aruch rules that the corners of a four-cornered garment may be nullified by clasping the two sides together across the lower half, and requires the fastening to sit well below the halfway mark so that an onlooker can see the garment is closed. From this the Mishnah Berurah warns against buckles on the sides of a tallis katan, but only where they are bent and fastened tightly enough that removing them would take a real act. Ordinary buttons open and close freely, and snap fasteners and zippers separate simply by pulling the sides apart, so none of them amounts to a connection and tzitzis may be attached to such garments. What remains is the concern of maris ayin, that an onlooker might think a bracha is being recited on a garment which is in fact closed. The Be’ur Halacha cites many who dismiss that worry as far-fetched, while the Shulchan Aruch HaRav and the Pesakei Teshuvos rule against wearing such a garment, noting that no concern arises at all when it is worn beneath one’s clothes.

sourceRef.snippet: If you just buckle the area on or around the 50% mark, there is an issue of maris ayin -- people will think that more than 50% is open and suspect you of wearing a four-cornered garment without tzitzis. Each corner carries four long strings folded in half into eight shorter ones. The Rosh invalidates the tzitzis only where one of the four long strings is severed at both ends without enough left for a slip knot. On his view a single shorter string tearing away is harmless, since its other half survives, and even two tearing away are acceptable where they are on the same side of the knot and the sides were kept from mixing, because they must then come from different long strings. Once five of the eight tear away without a slip knot’s length remaining, one long string is certainly cut at both ends and the tzitzis are invalid. Rabbeinu Tam is stricter, requiring two of the long strings to remain at their full length on both sides, which means four of the eight shorter strings. So where three of the shorter strings tear to less than the full length, whichever side they are on, the concern is that they come from three different long strings and leave only one intact, and the tzitzis are invalid. The Shulchan Aruch rules like the Rosh while saying that one should follow Rabbeinu Tam where possible, and the Rama records that the custom follows Rabbeinu Tam.

questions.modelAnswer: The Shulchan Aruch obliges a person to check his tzitzis before wearing them so that he does not say a bracha in vain, and the Mishnah Berurah adopts the stringencies of both the Taz and the Magen Avraham, so the area between the hole and the first knot is checked and every pair being worn is checked. The Mishnah Berurah adds that strings inspected before the tallis was put away need not be checked again the next morning, and the Aruch HaShulchan treats the whole requirement as a chumra that applies where there is time.

The Magen Avraham asks how the Shulchan Aruch can allow a bracha on a tallis taken without the owner's knowledge, since a borrower fulfills the mitzvah only where the garment is given to him as a matanah al menas lehachzir, and an owner who knows nothing of the loan has given nothing. He answers that the bracha here is permitted rather than required, exactly as a person who attaches tzitzis to a borrowed garment within thirty days may say a bracha on the strength of the ruling that a woman says a bracha on a time-bound mitzvah. When the Shulchan Aruch writes that one may recite a bracha on it, he means that it is permitted and not that it is obligatory. Rabbi Akiva Eiger objects on two grounds. First, the answer works only for the Rama, who allows a woman to say such a bracha; the Shulchan Aruch himself holds that she does not, so on his own view a bracha here should be forbidden. Second, even for Ashkenazim the comparison breaks down. A four-cornered garment without strings is exempt, and by attaching his own strings the borrower creates an obligation, much as a woman brings herself into a time-bound mitzvah. A tallis that already carries tzitzis is exempted outright by the Torah while it is borrowed, and nothing the borrower does can generate an obligation; only a matanah al menas lehachzir would help, and that cannot be made without the owner's knowledge. The Mishnah Berurah therefore rules like the Derech HaChaim that the borrower should have in mind not to acquire the tallis and should not say a bracha, and the Halacha Berurah rules likewise for Sephardim. The Piskei Teshuvos records the answer of the Shach and the Chazon Ish, that since a person is presumed pleased to have his property used for a mitzvah, his consent is taken to include whatever the mitzvah requires, so it is treated as though he had made the gift on condition of return.

sourceRef.snippet: When borrowing a four-cornered garment without strings, in essence the garment is exempt, but by placing your own strings on it, you create an obligation (similar to women who want to be obligated in a time-bound mitzvah). However, if you are borrowing a tallis with tzitzis attached, the Torah completely exempts such a garment, and there's nothing you can do to create that obligation. The only way a bracha may be recited is if it was given to you as a מתנה על מנת להחזיר (which cannot be done without the owner's knowledge).

questions.modelAnswer: The Shulchan Aruch requires a person to check his tzitzis before putting them on so that he does not say a bracha in vain. The Taz explains that although a chazakah would ordinarily allow us to assume that strings kosher yesterday are kosher today, the gravity of a bracha levatalah overrides the chazakah. The Magen Avraham gives a different account: a chazakah is relied on only where verification is impossible, and here the strings can easily be examined, and in any case they are prone to tear so the chazakah is weak. On his view both reasons are needed together. Three practical differences follow. Where a tallis katan is worn without a bracha because the bracha on the tallis gadol will cover it, the Taz sees no need to check, since no bracha is at stake, while the Magen Avraham still requires it, because the strings tear easily and can readily be checked. Where several pairs are put on together, the Taz requires checking only the pair on which the bracha is said, while the Magen Avraham requires each pair to be checked. And in the stretch between the hole and the first knot, the Taz requires checking because of the severity of a bracha levatalah, while the Magen Avraham does not, since tearing there is uncommon even though it is easy to inspect. The Mishnah Berurah rules stringently like both, so that area is checked and every pair is checked, though he adds that strings inspected before the tallis was put away need not be checked again in the morning. The Aruch HaShulchan traces the ruling to the Rosh, who treated it as a chumra and midas chassidus, and concludes that it applies only where there is time and that a tallis kept in a bag needs no check; Rav Ovadya rules similarly, and Rav Chaim Kanievsky requires a check where a bracha will be said and otherwise only a quick glance.

sourceRef.snippet: The משנ״ב passkins like both the ט״ז and מג״א le'chumra. Therefore, the משנ״ב סקכ״א passkins that one should check even the area between the hole and the first knot (like the ט״ז) and in סקכ״ב he passkins that when wearing many pairs of tzitzis (and when not reciting a bracha on the tallis katan because you will recite a bracha on the tallis gadol), you still need to check all the pairs of tzitzis (like the מג״א).

The Magen Avraham rejects the proof, suggesting that Dovid may well have slept without tzitzis and was untroubled because a mezuzah on his door left him with a mitzvah. The Shulchan HaTahor defends the Arizal, pointing out that for much of his life Dovid was a shepherd and then a warrior who slept in tents where there was no mezuzah, so his composure at night is best explained by his having slept in tzitzis; he concludes that a person sleeping in a house with a mezuzah need not sleep in tzitzis, while a traveller staying somewhere without one would do well to. The Shevet HaLevi holds that the reasons of the Arizal are kabbalistic and apply even in a house with a mezuzah. The Chazon Ish is reported not to have slept in his tzitzis, while the Halacha Berurah cites the Arizal in favour, and the practical guidance is to ask one's Rav. Separately, the Mishnah Berurah rules that a person who slept in his tallis katan should not say the bracha himself in the morning, because of the dispute between the Rosh and the Rambam over whether night is exempt from tzitzis or only a night garment is, and should instead be included in somebody else's bracha.
